INTERSTATE TRANSFER AND JURISDICTION OF ADULT CONSERVATORSHIPS (CALIFORNIA CONSERVATORSHIP JURISDICTION ACT) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Morgan T. Ellis · Jordan T. Reyes

THIS INFORMATION SHEET ADDRESSES WHICH STATE'S COURTS HAVE AUTHORITY, AND TRANSFER OF AN EXISTING CONSERVATORSHIP — NOT THE INITIAL CALIFORNIA PETITION
This information sheet describes a different subject from this corpus's companion document, "Conservatorship of an Adult — Petition Information Sheet." That document describes the process for establishing a brand-new California conservatorship over an adult who has no existing conservatorship anywhere. This document instead describes California's enactment of a modified version of the Uniform Adult Guardianship and Protective Proceedings Jurisdiction Act, cited under California law as the "California Conservatorship Jurisdiction Act" — the law that addresses which state's courts have authority to appoint or supervise a conservator for Morgan T. Ellis when Morgan T. Ellis has connections to more than one state, and the statutory process for transferring an existing conservatorship for Morgan T. Ellis into California from another state, or out of California to another state, without starting an entirely new proceeding from scratch. This document does not itself establish, transfer, or terminate any conservatorship, does not itself register any out-of-state order, and does not determine which state's courts actually have jurisdiction over Morgan T. Ellis's case; only a court order does that.

CALIFORNIA'S MODIFIED ENACTMENT OF THE UNIFORM ACT, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT COVER
By enacting Probate Code Division 4, Part 3, Chapter 8 (Probate Code §§ 1980-2033), the California Legislature stated its intent "to enact a modified version of the Uniform Adult Guardianship and Protective Proceedings Jurisdiction Act," and the chapter "may be cited as the 'California Conservatorship Jurisdiction Act.'" The chapter governs conservatorships of an adult; it does not apply to a minor, "regardless of whether the minor is or was married," and it does not apply to a guardianship proceeding for a minor. It also does not apply to a proceeding for involuntary commitment to a mental health facility or other involuntary mental health care, including proceedings under the Lanterman-Petris-Short Act and several enumerated Penal Code and Welfare and Institutions Code commitment schemes.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "By enacting this chapter, it is the Legislature’s intent to enact a modified version of the Uniform Adult Guardianship and Protective Proceedings Jurisdiction Act."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1980(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1980(a), (b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1980.)
  "This chapter may be cited as the “California Conservatorship Jurisdiction Act.”"
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1980(b) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1980(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1980.)
  "This chapter does not apply to a minor, regardless of whether the minor is or was married."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1981(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1981(a)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1981.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own enactment of a modified version of the Uniform Adult Guardianship and Protective Proceedings Jurisdiction Act and of that enactment's basic scope — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific proposed conservatee's case. Because California's version is expressly a "modified" version of the uniform act, this clause does not attempt to identify every respect in which California's text departs from the uniform act as originally drafted or as enacted in other states; a conservatorship with connections to another state may be governed differently there. This clause quotes only the minor and involuntary-commitment exclusions from § 1981(a)-(b); it does not quote the further exclusion in § 1981(c) for certain developmental-disability proceedings, addressed in this document's companion clause on registration. No case law search was performed for this clause: CourtListener's daily search quota (125 requests/day) was already exhausted at the time of this research (confirmed by a 429 rate-limit response before any substantive query was run), so this document is statute-only and discloses that choice rather than waiting out the quota.

"HOME STATE" AND "SIGNIFICANT-CONNECTION STATE" — THE TWO THRESHOLD TERMS THE JURISDICTION TEST TURNS ON
The jurisdictional test described in this document's companion clause depends on two defined terms. A proposed conservatee's "home state" means the state in which the proposed conservatee was physically present, including any period of temporary absence, for at least six consecutive months immediately before the filing of a petition for a conservatorship order — or, if none, the state where the proposed conservatee was so present for at least six consecutive months ending within the six months before the petition was filed. A "significant-connection state" means a state, other than the home state, with which the proposed conservatee has a significant connection other than mere physical presence, and in which substantial evidence concerning the proposed conservatee is available.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“Home state” means the state in which the proposed conservatee was physically present, including any period of temporary absence, for at least six consecutive months immediately before the filing of a petition for a conservatorship order, or, if none, the state in which the proposed conservatee was physically present, including any period of temporary absence, for at least six consecutive months ending within the six months prior to the filing of the petition."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1991(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1991(a)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1991.)
  "“Significant-connection state” means a state, other than the home state, with which a proposed conservatee has a significant connection other than mere physical presence and in which substantial evidence concerning the proposed conservatee is available."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1991(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1991(a)(3) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1991.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California's version of the uniform act defines these two threshold terms — not a claim about which state actually qualifies as any particular proposed conservatee's home state or a significant-connection state in any specific case; that depends on facts about that individual's own history of presence and ties to each state. This clause quotes only the two defined terms from § 1991(a)(2)-(3); it does not quote § 1991(a)(1)'s definition of "emergency" or the four-factor list in § 1991(b) that a court consults to decide whether a significant connection exists (family location, duration of presence, location of property, and ties such as voting registration, tax filings, vehicle registration, and driver's license). It also does not address § 1982's separate, broader set of chapter-wide definitions (for example, of "conservator," "conservatee," and "state," the last of which is defined to include a federally recognized Indian tribe, Puerto Rico, the District of Columbia, and other listed jurisdictions in addition to the fifty states). No case law search was performed for this clause because CourtListener's daily quota was already exhausted at the time of this research.

WHICH STATE'S COURTS MAY APPOINT A CONSERVATOR — THE EXCLUSIVE STATUTORY PRIORITY ORDER
For a conservatorship proceeding governed by this article, the statute "provides the exclusive basis for determining whether the courts of this state, as opposed to the courts of another state, have jurisdiction to appoint a conservator of the person, a conservator of the estate, or a conservator of the person and estate." Under that exclusive basis, a California court has jurisdiction to appoint a conservator for a proposed conservatee if California is the proposed conservatee's home state. If California is not the home state, a California court has jurisdiction if, on the date the petition is filed, California is a significant-connection state and the proposed conservatee does not have a home state at all. The statute goes on to provide further, lower-priority bases for California jurisdiction — including where the home state has expressly declined jurisdiction in California's favor, where no petition is pending elsewhere and no timely objection or competing petition is filed, and a residual "appropriate forum" basis where no other state has jurisdiction — as well as a separate, narrower category of special jurisdiction (for example, for a true emergency) addressed in a different section.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "For a conservatorship proceeding governed by this article, this article provides the exclusive basis for determining whether the courts of this state, as opposed to the courts of another state, have jurisdiction to appoint a conservator of the person, a conservator of the estate, or a conservator of the person and estate."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1992 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1992 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1992.)
  "A court of this state has jurisdiction to appoint a conservator for a proposed conservatee if this state is the proposed conservatee’s home state."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1993(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1993(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1993.)
  "A court of this state has jurisdiction to appoint a conservator for a proposed conservatee if, on the date the petition is filed, this state is a significant-connection state and the proposed conservatee does not have a home state."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1993(b) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1993(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1993.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's exclusive statutory jurisdiction test for appointing a conservator — not a claim about which state's courts actually have jurisdiction over any specific proposed conservatee. This clause quotes § 1992's exclusivity rule and § 1993(a)-(b), the two highest-priority jurisdictional bases (home state; significant-connection state with no home state); it does not quote the full text of § 1993(c)-(f), which set out three further, lower-priority bases and cross-reference the forum-appropriateness factors in § 1996 and the special jurisdiction described in § 1994. It also does not address § 1995 (a California court's exclusive and continuing jurisdiction once it has appointed a conservator), § 1996 (a California court's discretion to decline jurisdiction in favor of a more appropriate forum), § 1997 (the effect of unjustifiable conduct in acquiring jurisdiction), or the notice and simultaneous-petition rules of §§ 1998-1999. No case law search was performed for this clause because CourtListener's daily quota was already exhausted at the time of this research.

TRANSFERRING AN EXISTING CALIFORNIA CONSERVATORSHIP TO ANOTHER STATE
A conservator appointed in California, such as Jordan T. Reyes, "may petition the court to transfer the conservatorship to another state" — such as Nevada — rather than requiring the other state to start an entirely new conservatorship proceeding for Morgan T. Ellis from scratch. After notice and a hearing, a California court will issue only a provisional order granting the transfer, and only if the court is satisfied the conservatorship will be accepted by the other state's court and finds, among other things, that Morgan T. Ellis "is physically present in or is reasonably expected to move permanently to the other state," and that either no objection to the transfer has been made or, if one has, "the court determines that the transfer would not be contrary to the interests of the conservatee." A final order confirming the transfer and terminating the California conservatorship issues only after the receiving state's court has issued its own provisional order accepting the case, and the required termination documents (including any required accounting) have been filed in California.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A conservator appointed in this state may petition the court to transfer the conservatorship to another state."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 2001(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 2001(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=2001.)
  "The conservatee is physically present in or is reasonably expected to move permanently to the other state."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 2001(d)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 2001(d)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=2001.)
  "An objection to the transfer has not been made or, if an objection has been made, the court determines that the transfer would not be contrary to the interests of the conservatee."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 2001(d)(2) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 2001(d)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=2001.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual outbound-transfer petition process available to an existing California conservator — not advice that transfer to any particular state is appropriate for any particular conservatee, and not a guarantee that another state's courts will accept the transfer. This clause quotes only § 2001(a) and one physical-presence finding and one objection finding drawn from § 2001(d) (the findings required for transferring a conservatorship of the person); it does not quote the parallel but not identical findings required for a conservatorship of the estate under § 2001(e) (which also allows a significant-connection basis, not only physical presence or an expected permanent move), the combined-findings rule of § 2001(f) for a conservatorship of the person and estate, or the exact final-order mechanics of § 2001(g). It also does not address § 1981(c)'s exclusion of certain developmental-disability proceedings from this transfer article, or § 2003's special rule for transfers to or from a California tribe's court. No case law search was performed for this clause because CourtListener's daily quota was already exhausted at the time of this research.

ACCEPTING AN EXISTING OUT-OF-STATE CONSERVATORSHIP TRANSFERRED INTO CALIFORNIA
The mirror-image process applies when a conservatorship for Morgan T. Ellis was established in another state, such as Texas, and that state's court has already issued a provisional order transferring the case out. "To confirm transfer of a conservatorship transferred to this state under provisions similar to Section 2001, the conservator shall petition the court in this state to accept the conservatorship," and "[t]he petition shall include a certified copy of the other state's provisional order of transfer." The California court must appoint an investigator to conduct a preliminary investigation, hold a hearing, and will grant only a provisional order accepting the case unless it finds the transfer would be contrary to Morgan T. Ellis's interests, that Jordan T. Reyes is ineligible to serve as conservator under either the transferring state's law or California law without an identified eligible replacement, or that the chapter does not apply. A final order accepting the proceeding and appointing the conservator in California issues only after a further conformity determination and review confirming the conservatorship complies with California law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "To confirm transfer of a conservatorship transferred to this state under provisions similar to Section 2001, the conservator shall petition the court in this state to accept the conservatorship."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 2002(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 2002(a)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=2002.)
  "The petition shall include a certified copy of the other state’s provisional order of transfer."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 2002(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 2002(a)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=2002.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual inbound-transfer acceptance process available once another state's court has provisionally granted an outbound transfer — not advice that transfer into California is appropriate for any particular conservatee, and not a claim that a California court will necessarily accept any particular transfer. This clause quotes only § 2002(a)(1)-(2); it does not quote the notice requirements of § 2002(b), the full list of grounds on which a person may object under § 2002(c), the investigator and hearing requirements of § 2002(d)-(e), the full list of grounds on which the court must deny provisional acceptance under § 2002(f), the post-provisional 60-day conformity-determination and review process of § 2002(h), or the final-order and effective-date rules of § 2002(i) (including the specific pre-effectiveness steps: the conservator's oath, any required bond, delivery of the information required by § 1835, and issuance of letters of conservatorship). No case law search was performed for this clause because CourtListener's daily quota was already exhausted at the time of this research.

REGISTERING AN OUT-OF-STATE CONSERVATORSHIP ORDER IN CALIFORNIA IS A NARROWER, DIFFERENT TOOL THAN TRANSFERRING THE CASE
Separately from the transfer process described in this document's other clauses, California law gives an out-of-state conservator a narrower option: registering the existing out-of-state order in a California superior court without moving the underlying conservatorship proceeding itself. Where a conservator of the person has been appointed for Morgan T. Ellis in another state, such as Texas, and no California petition for a conservator of the person is pending, that conservator, after providing the required notice, "may register the conservatorship order in this state by filing certified copies of the order and letters of office, and proof of notice as required herein, together with a cover sheet approved by the Judicial Council, in the superior court of any appropriate county of this state." Registration lets Jordan T. Reyes exercise the out-of-state order's powers in California — for example, over property Morgan T. Ellis owns here — while Morgan T. Ellis continues to reside in the other state; the underlying conservatorship remains supervised by Texas's court, which the California case (D-1-FM-24-001234) is not replacing. That registered authority is expressly conditional on where Morgan T. Ellis actually resides: it "applies only when the conservatee resides out of this state," and "[w]hen the conservatee resides in this state, a conservator may not exercise any powers pursuant to a registration under this article."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "If a conservator of the person has been appointed in another state and a petition for the appointment of a conservator of the person is not pending in this state, the conservator of the person appointed in the other state, after providing notice pursuant to Section 2014, may register the conservatorship order in this state by filing certified copies of the order and letters of office, and proof of notice as required herein, together with a cover sheet approved by the Judicial Council, in the superior court of any appropriate county of this state."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 2011 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 2011 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=2011.)
  "Subdivision (a) applies only when the conservatee resides out of this state. When the conservatee resides in this state, a conservator may not exercise any powers pursuant to a registration under this article."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 2016(c) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 2016(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=2016.)

This clause quotes only § 2011 (registration for a conservator of the person) and § 2016(c); it does not quote the parallel registration provisions for a conservator of the estate (§ 2012) or of the person and estate (§ 2013), the advance-notice requirements of § 2014, the written-information and fee provisions of § 2015, the rest of § 2016 (including the requirement to seek California court approval before taking an action that would require it under California law, and the specific California statutes listed there that impose special requirements on a registered conservator), the good-faith third-party reliance protection of § 2017, the recordation option of § 2018, or the special rules for a California tribe's order under § 2019. No case law search was performed for this clause because CourtListener's daily quota was already exhausted at the time of this research.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT AND SIGNATURE BLOCK — INTERSTATE TRANSFER AND JURISDICTION INFORMATION SHEET
I, Jordan T. Reyes, have reviewed this information sheet in connection with a conservatorship concerning Morgan T. Ellis, presently associated with the following case information: issuing state Texas, issuing court District Court of Travis County, Texas, case number D-1-FM-24-001234. I understand this information sheet describes California's statutory framework for interstate jurisdiction, transfer, and registration of adult conservatorships under Probate Code §§ 1980-2033, and that it is not itself a petition, transfer order, registration filing, or any other court document. Signing this information sheet does not transfer, register, modify, or terminate any conservatorship, and does not itself establish which state's courts have jurisdiction over Morgan T. Ellis's case; only a court order does that.

I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing is true and correct.

Executed on September 1, 2026 at Oakland, California.

Signature of Jordan T. Reyes: ☐ _________________________

Ellis was established in another state, such as Texas, and that state's court has already issued a provisional order transferring the case out. "To confirm transfer of a conservatorship transferred to this state under provisions similar to Section 2001, the conservator shall petition the court in this state to accept the conservatorship," and "[t]he petition shall include a certified copy of the other state's provisional order of transfer." The California court must appoint an investigator to conduct a preliminary investigation, hold a hearing, and will grant only a provisional order accepting the case unless it finds the transfer would be contrary to Morgan T. Ellis's interests, that Jordan T. Reyes is ineligible to serve as conservator under either the transferring state's law or California law without an identified eligible replacement, or that the chapter does not apply. A final order accepting the proceeding and appointing the conservator in California issues only after a further conformity determination and review confirming the conservatorship complies with California law.

expectedJSON.body: Separately from the transfer process described in this document's other clauses, California law gives an out-of-state conservator a narrower option: registering the existing out-of-state order in a California superior court without moving the underlying conservatorship proceeding itself. Where a conservator of the person has been appointed for Morgan T. Ellis in another state, such as Texas, and no California petition for a conservator of the person is pending, that conservator, after providing the required notice, "may register the conservatorship order in this state by filing certified copies of the order and letters of office, and proof of notice as required herein, together with a cover sheet approved by the Judicial Council, in the superior court of any appropriate county of this state." Registration lets Jordan T. Reyes exercise the out-of-state order's powers in California — for example, over property Morgan T. Ellis owns here — while Morgan T. Ellis continues to reside in the other state; the underlying conservatorship remains supervised by Texas's court, which the California case (D-1-FM-24-001234) is not replacing. That registered authority is expressly conditional on where Morgan T. Ellis actually resides: it "applies only when the conservatee resides out of this state," and "[w]hen the conservatee resides in this state, a conservator may not exercise any powers pursuant to a registration under this article."
